dialogue.content: I spent the first hour tidying the tasting notes and closing stale entries.
The cellar list review wrapped early today.
Table-side improvisation with guests over a list I built is effortless.
Improvising on your own terrain works.
My terrain, my vintages, no fear.
Someone new shadowed me in the dining room this morning.
A little, but the questions were good ones.
I batched my replies about the flight design into one message before lunch.
My guided tastings succeed because I design the flight and write the notes in advance; the food press named the autumn flight the city's best precisely for that structure.
The designed format is your named strength.
Radio interviews about the cellar, with topics agreed ahead, have gone smoothly.
I archived last cycle's notes on the cellar list and set up the new folder.
As fresh as these things get.
The restaurant's booking spike after that review came almost entirely through the tasting-menu channel.
A vendor call about the tasting notes ran long but ended well.
I walked through the dining room checklist with the new starter.
Careful and quick, a good sign.
Quiet afternoon; I cleared the backlog around the flight design.
I flagged a small inconsistency in the cellar list records and fixed it at the source.
The one live blind-tasting I did on radio went sideways: I misidentified a vintage under the clock and the clip still circulates in the trade groups.
One live blind format, one circulating clip.
I sketched next week's plan for the flight design before leaving.
Lunch walk, then a clean pass through the tasting notes updates.
The television offer is a weekly live blind-tasting segment under studio time pressure, exactly the radio format with cameras added.
The offer is the failure format, amplified.
I compared two options for the cellar list tooling and noted a mild preference.
I closed the week by updating the dining room handover notes.
If I accept the weekly live blind-tasting segment as offered, how does my first season on air realistically go?
